new_statements.quote: There are three indications that the original stress system in Umpithamu must have been one that was left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule. The first indication is local, relating to Umpithamu’s closest relatives. Most other Middle Paman languages for which we have a reliable description of word stress have a system of this kind: this is the case, for instance, in Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988).
new_statements.citation: Verstraete, Jean-Christophe. 2021. Stress change and initial consonant loss in Umpithamu: cause or consequence? Transactions of the Philological Society 119(2): 152-173 (DOI 10.1111/1467-968X.12210), sec. 3.3 — reporting Smith & Johnson 2000 second-hand. Corroborated second-hand by Blevins 2025: 142 ('following a short initial stressed syllable', after Smith & Johnson 2000).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: lines 602-607 (author's accepted MS p.17, sec. 3.3 'Diachronic implications') carries the quoted passage word for word ('There are three indications... left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule... Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988)'); the only omission is the footnote call '5' after '(Thompson 1988)'. MS p.19 (15a) restates the Middle Paman starting point as 'Left-to-right parsing, leftmost stress rule'. This is a typological classification citing Smith & Johnson 2000, i.e. second-hand. Corroboration re-read: Blevins 2025 (langsci 415) p.142, PDF p.150, in../wiki1239/: Kugu Nganhca…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per second-hand reports of Smith & Johnson's (2000) Handbook description, Kugu Nganhcara (the patrilect cluster that includes Kugu Muminh) has left-aligned word stress with primary stress on the initial syllable; Blevins (2025:142), citing the same source, adds that consonants other than /r/ optionally geminate after a short initial stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported in the accessible (second-hand) sources.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the second-hand reports. (Smith & Johnson 1986:35 state the patrilects, incl. Muminh, differ 'in only minor aspects of their... phonology', so a Kugu Nganhcara statement should hold for Muminh; Evans 1995 snippet notes Kugu-Nganhcara is syllable-timed rather than stress-timed.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress as characterised typologically ('leftmost stress rule'); no information on phrase level, clitics or citation forms in the accessible text. The primary statement (Smith & Johnson 2000, Handbook of Australian Languages 5, phonology section) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All stress reports are for 'Kugu Nganhcara' (Smith & Johnson's cover term for six mutually intelligible patrilects: Kugu Uwanh kuku1280, Kugu Ugbanh kuku1281, Kugu Mu'inh kuku1282, Kugu Muminh kuku1283, Kugu Yi'anh, Wik Iyanh wiki1239; ISO/WALS 'knc/wua' Wikngenchera wikn1246), not for Kugu Muminh individually. Smith & Johnson 1986:35 state the patrilects 'are identical in syntax and differ in only minor aspects of their morphology and phonology', so a Kugu Nganhcara stress statement should apply to kuku1283. Kugu Muminh = 'Wik Muminh' in Hale's 1960 notes; often equated with/close to Wik-Me'nh (wikm1246) in older sources, but Sutton & Hale 2021 treat them as distinct.
